entry.title: SIX CONTESTS END WITH THE HOME NINE STORMING THE PLATE, AND THE GRANDEST FINISH BELONGS TO PHILADELPHIA: BOHM'S TRIPLE IN THE TENTH, PHILLIES 7, CARDINALS 6
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 45 · Saturday, the Two-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX CONTESTS END WITH THE HOME NINE STORMING THE PLATE, AND THE GRANDEST FINISH BELONGS TO PHILADELPHIA: BOHM'S TRIPLE IN THE TENTH, PHILLIES 7, CARDINALS 6

On a night when fully six of the card's fifteen engagements were settled by the last man to swing, the Philadelphias fall behind in the tenth upon Fermín's single, whereupon Bohm lashes the first three-bagger of his season to the deepest quarter of the yard, Harper and Sosa come racing home, and the winning streak stretches to seven

From the Delaware to the Puget Sound, Friday night's dispatches all arrived written in the same hand: the home nine batting last, the winning run crossing in the game's final turn. Six times it happened — in Philadelphia, in Miami, on the South Side of Chicago, in Arlington, in Seattle, and in Los Angeles, each finish chronicled in its proper place below — and the fattest prize of the six was contested in Philadelphia, where the Cardinals and the Phillies traded the lead like men passing a hot stone until the tenth inning finally burned the visitors' hands.

St. Louis struck first, Joshua Báez lifting a two-run homer, his fourth, in the opening frame with Jordan Walker aboard. The Philadelphias pecked their way back against the starter Dobbins — Marsh and Realmuto doubling home runs in the second, Bohm singling home a third in the third — and when Walker answered in the sixth with a two-run blast of his own, his seven-and-twentieth, the home men replied within the half-hour: Realmuto's second double and Crawford's sacrifice fly turned four-to-three into four-to-five. Bryan Torres tied the affair with a single in the eighth, the ninth passed without a verdict, and in the tenth José Fermín — the same Fermín whose two-run single crowned Thursday's larceny in Cincinnati, as this paper related only yesterday — lined the go-ahead run home, and the ninth-inning miracle workers of St. Louis appeared poised to bank a tenth-inning sequel. But Alec Bohm, who had already driven in one run and knocked at the door all evening, met the reliever Gastelum with a sharp drive to the center-field expanse — the first triple of his season, and no man was catching it — and Harper and Sosa crossed with the tying and winning runs while the yard came apart.

The ledger reads richly for the victors: three runs driven in for Bohm, a pair of doubles for Realmuto, nine strikeouts for the starter Luzardo in five and two-thirds, and a seventh consecutive victory — eight in ten — that holds the National's second wild-card chair by two full games and draws Philadelphia within four of Atlanta, beaten at Milwaukee as the columns below attest. For St. Louis the arithmetic is crueler: Walker's two runs driven in lift him to six-and-ninety, a full share of the major-league lead as the milestone desk reports, but the club that stole a game from its last strike on Thursday gave one back from the brink of victory on Friday, and sits three and a half games from the league's final chair. McFarlane took the decision, Gastelum the defeat, and the two nines resume the argument at Citizens Bank Park this very evening.

News Around the League

THE MARTE AFFAIR, CONTINUED: LOVULLO SPEAKS OF BETRAYAL AND OF PEACE IN THE SAME BREATH

The strangest story of the week, chronicled in these columns since Tuesday, acquired its next chapter Friday in Phoenix, where the manager Torey Lovullo walked the finest of lines in his first full accounting of the business — the second baseman Ketel Marte's failure to appear at Fenway Park, the restricted list, and Thursday's long audience at Salt River Fields that this paper described yesterday. The wires report that Lovullo confessed to feeling betrayed by the disappearance, even as he pronounced the Thursday summit worthwhile: 'I thought it was a very productive meeting,' he offered, declining every invitation to particulars that both sides wish kept private, and expressing the hope that all parties may now get back to the baseball. The club's interest in that outcome is not small: the Sonoran nine won again Friday, as the card below relates, and sit a single game from the National's final chair with their second baseman serving out his ten days on the shelf.

THE PROSPECT DESK: THE WATCH ENDS THIS EVENING — ANDERSON TAKES A MAJOR-LEAGUE MOUND AT LAST

The watch this paper opened yesterday closes on schedule. The Mariners' manager Dan Wilson confirmed Friday that Kade Anderson, the left-hander of two-and-twenty years whom the Pipeline scribes rank the finest pitching pupil in all the minors and the fifth prospect of any description, will make his debut this evening in Seattle against the Cubs. The occasion carries its own history: by the researchers' accounting he becomes but the sixteenth pitching prospect ranked among the game's five best to step onto a major-league mound in the twenty-odd years such rankings have been kept. The summons required some shuffling of the watch bill — Bryan Woo's turn has been pushed back, though the club expects no visit to the injured list, and the reliever Carlos Vargas was activated besides. A club three games from the American's final chair, and fresh from the extra-inning deliverance the card below describes, could scarcely have timed the reinforcement better.

THE MILESTONE DESK: WALKER DRAWS LEVEL WITH THE ROOKIE AT SIX-AND-NINETY, AND ALVAREZ'S CROWN OF THREE HOLDS

The race this desk examined at length only yesterday is now a dead heat. Jordan Walker's two runs driven in at Philadelphia — a homer and more, as the lead dispatch relates — lift him to six-and-ninety on the season, drawing him precisely level with the Reds' rookie Sal Stewart, whose club was whitewashed in Phoenix and could offer its young colossus nothing to drive home. Atop all baseball they sit together, with Alec Burleson — Walker's own clubmate — lurking at three-and-ninety, and the question of whether a freshman may lead the major leagues in runs batted in, a thing done by no rookie since 1950, now hangs on a two-horse finish conducted largely within the same division. In the American, meanwhile, the desk renews its report that Yordan Alvarez holds every table that matters: two more doubles Friday in Houston's whitewash of the Athletics left his figures at .321, six-and-thirty homers, and ninety runs driven in — first in average, first in homers, first in runs batted in — and the pursuit of the batter's Triple Crown, unclaimed in the American since 2012, proceeds unbothered.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: PAGES' BROKEN HAND DIMS A CHAMPION'S SEPTEMBER, TOGLIA'S SHOULDER, AND TWO RETURNS PROMISED FOR THIS VERY DAY

The gravest entry issues from Los Angeles, where the All-Star center fielder Andy Pages took a pitch off the left hand in Friday's victory and the examination found a fracture: the wires report an absence of no fewer than four weeks, though the manager Roberts holds to the expectation that his man returns before the season's books are closed. In Phoenix the Reds' Michael Toglia departed in the first inning after a diving catch dislocated his right shoulder, a frightening scene the card below notes. But the ward also has discharges to announce, both promised for this very day: Vladimir Guerrero Jr., whose thunderous rehearsal at Dunedin this paper saluted yesterday, has passed his final concussion examinations and is expected to rejoin the Blue Jays in the Bronx this afternoon, the first day the seven-day list allows; and the Yankees' Max Fried is scheduled to throw from a mound for the first time since the bone bruise in his left elbow returned him to the shelf — a rehearsal, not a return, but the direction is the right one.

THE COUNTING-HOUSE DESK: KASTEN PRONOUNCES THE CHAMPIONS NOT FOR SALE, AND THE HERALD CONSULTS THE LEDGER BEFORE JOINING ANY CHOIR

The president of the champion Dodgers, Stan Kasten, spent part of Friday extinguishing a rumor: amid speculation abroad on the wires concerning the club's future under the owner Mark Walter, Kasten assured the faithful that the franchise is not for sale, and there the matter rests.

The desk pairs the item with the ticking of the labor clock, which grows daily harder to ignore: the collective bargaining agreement between the owners and the players expires on the first of December, the parties having opened their negotiations in May, and the owners' men have already begun rehearsing the old hymn of competitive balance — by which is generally meant, once the verses are parsed, a ceiling upon what a ballplayer may be paid. The Herald has taken the precaution of consulting the ledger before joining the choir, and the ledger declines to weep. By Forbes' own published accounting, not one of the thirty franchises is valued below a thousand millions of dollars — the humblest of them, the Miami club, is prized at a billion and better, and the grandest, the Yankees of New York, at eight billions and two hundred millions — figures that have grown handsomer nearly every year the accountants have kept them. And as for the pennant races the proposed ceiling is advertised to rescue, the postseason record wants no rescuing: seven different champions have carried off the flag in the last ten autumns, the 2023 Series was contested by two wild-card nines — one of them with but four-and-eighty wins to its name — and the best record in all of last season's baseball was posted at Milwaukee, among the smallest of the game's markets. The Herald's sympathies in matters of the purse lie, and will lie, with the men who play the games; it will follow the ledger so its readers need not, and it commends the same arithmetic to the owners' negotiators, who can well afford the subscription.

The Rest of the Card

THE TWO SOVEREIGNS OF THE EARNED-RUN TABLE MEET, AND THE YOUNGER MAN PREVAILS: MILWAUKEES 2, BRAVES 1

The engagement of the weekend, advertised in yesterday's bill of fare, delivered everything but runs. Jacob Misiorowski threw scoreless ball at Chris Sale and the East's leaders, ran his record to thirteen-and-five with his earned-run figure at a scandalous 1.68 and his strikeout count at two hundred sixteen — the National's finest on both counts — and drew from the vanquished Sale afterward a compliment of the very highest order regarding the young man's fastball. The scoring was modest work: Contreras singled home one in the third and Vaughn forced home another, Harris' single in the eighth drew Atlanta within a run, and Megill barred the door for his four-and-twentieth save — though the visitors' evening did include Acuña throwing out the rookie Lara at second base with a peg the instruments clocked at better than ninety-two miles per hour. Milwaukee, at eighty wins against nine-and-forty defeats, owns the finest ledger in baseball by two games; the same two clubs meet again this afternoon before repairing to Williamsport on the morrow.

FOUR HITS SUFFICE WHEN SCHLITTLER DEALS: YANKEES 3, JAYS 1, AND THE STREAK RUNS TO FIVE

Cam Schlittler, proprietor of the American's finest earned-run figure and Friday night of cleats honoring both the Light Side and the Dark, held Toronto to a single tally while his mates made four hits stretch a very long way: Spencer Jones' two-run homer in the second — upheld when the umpires reviewed it — and Caballero's sacrifice fly were the whole account, with Kirk's run-scoring single the visitors' lone reply and Bednar sealing his thirtieth save. The eleventh victory for Schlittler; a fifth consecutive for the Yankees, who sit three games behind the Rays — beaten in Baltimore, as the next item relates — and hold the American's first wild-card chair at a comfortable remove. The Jays expect reinforcement this very afternoon, as the infirmary column reports.

DEVERS RETURNS TO FENWAY AND HOMERS, BUT CONTRERAS HAS THE LOUDER ARGUMENT: HUB NINE 6, FRISCO NINE 4

The return of Rafael Devers to the yard he graced for the better part of a decade supplied the evening's theatre — the visitor declared himself 'very happy to be back,' declined every invitation to relitigate the parting, and proved the sentiment genuine with a homer to the center-field expanse, his six-and-twentieth. But the crowd of thirty-seven thousand reserved its fullest voice for the present tenant of the middle of Boston's order: Willson Contreras answered with a three-run blast of his own, likewise his six-and-twentieth, the centerpiece of a five-run third that also collected a bases-loaded walk and a hit batsman, and Abreu's triple added a sixth run later. Sonny Gray pitched to his sixteenth victory against three defeats — no man in the American owns more — with Chapman closing his eight-and-twentieth save, and the Hub nine hold the league's second wild-card chair at a comfortable remove; the Frisco nine, whatever their traveler's consolations, have dropped two running.

ALONSO'S THIRTIETH, FAIR BEYOND ALL ARGUMENT: BIRDS 5, TAMPA MEN 3

Two nights after the long strike that a review declined to make a homer — recorded in Thursday's edition of this paper — Pete Alonso removed the umpires from the conversation entirely, hammering his thirtieth of the season far inside the left-center bleachers with a man aboard, and adding a run-scoring single besides for three driven in and five-and-eighty on the year, second in the American. The Rays' account was not without its charm — Kenny Piper, a name new to these columns, struck his first homer of the year — but Rogers held the line for his ninth victory and Garcia closed the door. The league's best club has now dropped two running, its lead over the surging Yankees down to three; Baltimore, winners of one, will take its dignities where it finds them.

THREE HOMERS IN THE SIXTH, AND ROGERS — FOUR CLUBS AND COUNTING — ENDS IT IN THE NINTH: SOUTH SIDERS 6, METROPOLITANS 4

Down four runs to nothing after Bichette's thirteenth homer, the Central's leaders staged their recovery all in one frame: Vargas' two-run blast, his nine-and-twentieth, followed in short order by Grichuk and by Colson Montgomery, three homers in a single sixth inning to square the affair. There it stood until the ninth, when Jake Rogers — a catcher claimed off the waiver wire from Boston but a week ago, and the owner of base hits in four different uniforms this season — deposited a two-run homer into the center-field seats with two out, one of the night's six walk-off endings and surely the least probable. The South Siders hold first place in the American's Central; the Metropolitans have lost the services of the evening and, at eight-and-fifty wins, very nearly the season.

SANOJA TIES IT IN THE EIGHTH AND ENDS IT IN THE NINTH: FISH 3, NATS 2

Keibert Ruiz's sixth-inning homer stood as the game's only run until the eighth, when Javier Sanoja singled home the equalizer and Otto Lopez singled home the lead; Washington answered through Lile's run-scoring knock in the ninth, and so Sanoja simply did it again — a ground-ball single through the middle with the sacks occupied, his second run driven home of the night. Fairbanks took the decision. The Fish, winners of nine-and-thirty at their own yard this season, sit four games from the National's final chair; the Washingtons have dropped eight of ten.

WESNESKI'S LONG ROAD BACK RUNS THROUGH FIVE SPOTLESS INNINGS: ASTROS 4, A'S 0

The road home from the surgeon's table is rarely straight, but Hayden Wesneski made it look so Friday: five scoreless innings in his continuing return from the elbow operation, three Athletics hits all evening, and a whitewash that keeps Houston's grip on the West's first chair — one game over Texas, whose own evening is sung below. Yordan Alvarez doubled twice and drove in a run with each, commerce the milestone desk records in full, and Paredes doubled home another. The wandering A's have now lost five running, and at nine-and-forty wins the arithmetic of their season no longer requires a mathematician.

TO INFINITY, AND OVER THE FENCE: MISSOURIANS 5, MOTOR CITY NINE 2, AND THE STREAK REACHES SIX

The liveliest late August in the American's lower reaches rolls on. Kyle Isbel, armed for Players' Weekend with a bat done up in the livery of one Buzz Lightyear, sent a fifth-inning pitch to infinity and beyond the right-center fence, then doubled home an insurance run in the eighth; Pasquantino and the young catcher Jensen supplied homers of their own, and Cameron pitched to his eighth victory with Pearson closing. Six consecutive victories for Kansas City, whose season, whatever its ledger, refuses to go quietly; Detroit has dropped three running and slips two and a half games from the American's final chair, which the item below concerns directly.

NINE INNINGS OF NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING AT ONCE: TEXAS NINE 2, ANGELS 1, IN TEN, AND THE CHAIR IS RECLAIMED

For nine full innings at Arlington neither club scored a run, and then the tenth spent the whole evening's allowance in minutes: the Angels' Guzman doubled home the go-ahead man, whereupon Wyatt Langford answered with a two-bagger of his own to square it and Ezequiel Duran grounded a sharp single past third to bring Langford home with the verdict, an errant throw chasing the play — another of the night's six walk-off endings. Alexander claimed the decision over Joyce. Eleven hits the Texas nine collected while waiting for two to matter; the reward is sole possession of the American's final wild-card chair, of which the desk note gives the full accounting.

FOUR HITS FOR BAZZANA, AND TWO IN A ROW AT LAST: CLEVELAND NINE 9, MOUNTAIN MEN 1

The rookie Travis Bazzana, whose up-and-down freshman campaign the wires have chronicled since its hot start and All-Star nod, enjoyed the finest night of his young service: four hits and three driven in, the centerpiece of a rout in the thin Denver air that gave Cleveland consecutive victories for the first time in a month. Halpin homered, Patrick Bailey added a three-run shot in the seventh, and Herrin took the decision as Colorado managed a single first-inning tally. The Cleveland nine sit one game from the American's final chair — one of six clubs within two and a half of it, as the desk note relates — while the Mountain men, at fifty wins, play out the string with what grace the altitude allows.

LAWLAR'S THUNDER AND A WHITEWASH IN THE DESERT: SONORAN NINE 9, REDLEGS 0

Whatever weight the week's troubles have laid upon Arizona, none of it showed Friday: Jordan Lawlar homered early and finished with three driven in, seven different men drove home at least one, and Rodriguez pitched to his thirteenth victory against four defeats while Cincinnati was blanked entire. The evening's one dark passage came in the first inning, when the Redlegs' Toglia dislocated a shoulder completing a diving catch, a casualty the infirmary ward records. The Sonoran nine, winners of two running amid the Marte affair the news columns continue, sit one game from the National's final chair; the Redlegs' young colossus Stewart, held without a run to drive home, watched his share of the batting lead become a partnership, as the milestone desk explains.

A BAGUETTE IS BROKEN OVER A FORMER EMPLOYER: FRIARS 6, TWIN CITIES NINE 2

Ty France, bearing a Players' Weekend bat got up to resemble nothing so much as a Parisian loaf, greeted his former club in the first inning with a two-run homer — his eighteenth, and surely the best-dressed — and later added a sacrifice fly in a four-run fifth built of singles from Tatis, Rengifo, and Machado, three driven in for the evening. Clemens' two-run triple had briefly squared matters for Minnesota before Vásquez settled in for his ninth victory. The Friars hold the National's third wild-card chair with seven victories in ten; the Twin Cities nine, beaten from the American's final chair by Texas's late heroics, wake this morning a game behind it.

BREGMAN TIES IT TWICE, BUT RIVAS HAS THE FINAL SYLLABLE: SEATTLE NINE 6, NORTH SIDERS 5, IN TEN

Before the largest home gathering of Seattle's season, the Cubs struck first and hardest — Crow-Armstrong's two-and-thirtieth homer leading off, Bregman following at once with a two-run blast — and Cal Raleigh answered with a three-run shot in a four-run second. When Happ and then Bregman again, in the ninth, hauled Chicago level at five, the affair went to a tenth, where Leo Rivas lined a single to center and Arozarena came home with one more of the night's six walk-off verdicts. The evening's footnote belongs to the visitors' manager Counsell, ejected over a balk call on his own birthday. The North Siders have dropped two running, their grip on the National's first wild-card chair trimmed to five games; the Seattle nine hand the ball this evening to the debutant Anderson, as the prospect desk proclaims.

EDMAN SUPPLIES THE SWEET ENDING, THOUGH THE NIGHT EXACTS A PRICE: TROLLEY DODGERS 5, SMOKY CITY NINE 4, IN TEN

Muncy's two-run homer and Betts' two-run single staked Los Angeles early, Yamamoto turned in another quality start, and still it required extra work: Oneil Cruz squared the account at four with a two-run blast in the eighth, and the game rolled scoreless into the tenth until Tommy Edman lined a single to left, Enrique Hernández crossed, and Friday's ledger of walk-off verdicts reached six. Phillips claimed the decision. A fourth consecutive victory keeps the champions two games behind Milwaukee on the game's best ledger and comfortably atop the West — but the celebration was cut with worry, for the examination of Pages' hand, struck by a pitch mid-game, returned the fracture the infirmary ward reports in full.

The arithmetic desk reports that the American's final wild-card chair has now changed its arrangement on six consecutive mornings of this paper: Baltimore alone on Monday, three cotenants Tuesday, Texas alone Wednesday, Minnesota alone Thursday, Texas and Minnesota in shared occupancy yesterday — and this morning Texas alone once more, the tenth-inning deliverance at Arlington evicting its own cotenant, with the Twins and Guardians a game astern, Toronto a game and a half, Baltimore two, Detroit two and a half, and Seattle three, still not one claimant at the break-even line. In the National the seating holds: the Cubs keep the first chair by five games, Philadelphia — winners of seven running after the morning's lead dispatch — the second by two, San Diego the third, with Arizona one game back, St. Louis three and a half, and Miami four. This day is the second of Players' Weekend, given over by the program to the causes the players champion, and the card again runs to the full fifteen engagements. The bill of fare: in Seattle at 7:15 Eastern, the engagement of the evening — the debutant Anderson against the Cubs, the finest pitching prospect in the minors making his first bow, as the prospect desk relates; in the Bronx at 1:35, Cease and his two hundred one strikeouts visit Weathers, with Guerrero expected back in the visitors' line; at Milwaukee at 2:10, the Braves seek their revenge upon Henderson and his 2.70; at Philadelphia at 6:05, the young Painter takes the ball against the Cardinals with the streak at seven; at Baltimore at 7:05, McClanahan opposes Young and his nine victories; and at Los Angeles at 7:15, Skubal is charged with keeping the champions rolling against the Bucs. On the morrow the Brewers and Braves repair to Williamsport for the Little League Classic, at 7:10 in the evening, there to perform before the smallest and sternest jury in baseball, precisely as this paper has been promising all week. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE FINAL OUT FALLS OUT OF A GLOVE, AND SIX RUNS POUR THROUGH THE HOLE: CARDINALS 10, REDS 9, IN A NINTH INNING OF TEN RUNS AND NO MERCY
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 44 · Friday, the One-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 9 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE FINAL OUT FALLS OUT OF A GLOVE, AND SIX RUNS POUR THROUGH THE HOLE: CARDINALS 10, REDS 9, IN A NINTH INNING OF TEN RUNS AND NO MERCY

Down to their last out and trailing by one at Cincinnati, the St. Louis nine are reprieved when the center fielder Myers drops Wetherholt's routine fly — six runs follow at once — whereupon the Reds answer with four of their own and send the grand-slam man McLain to the plate with the bases full, only to watch Walker, author of the early lead, squeeze the game's last breath at the right-field wall

Of all the entries in a scorebook none is more contemptuous than the routine fly ball — the out so assured that the crowd reaches for its hats before the ball comes down. Thursday afternoon at Great American Ball Park, with two out in the ninth, the Cardinals trailing five-to-four, and the pinch-hitter Pereira just struck out for what should have been the penultimate indignity, JJ Wetherholt lofted precisely that entry toward left-center. Dane Myers ranged a long way to call off TJ Friedl, who had entered only an inning before as a defensive substitution, and the ball struck his leather and fell to the grass. Two runs crossed on the drop — the tying and the go-ahead — and the inning, thus pried open, would not be shut: Burleson singled home a seventh run, Joshua Báez walked with the bases full for an eighth, and José Fermín, who had scored the tying run moments earlier and came round to bat a second time in the frame, lined a two-run single for ten-to-five. Six runs, every one of them after the game stood a strike from ending.

The Reds declined to accept the verdict quietly. The manager Marmol, hoping to spare his closer a day's work amid a grinding stretch, entrusted the five-run cushion to Soriano, and the cushion was promptly devoured: Eugenio Suárez singled home one, the rookie Sal Stewart lined a two-run stroke — his six-and-ninetieth run driven in, a figure examined at length in the news columns — and Stephenson walked with the sacks full to draw within a single tally. So Riley O'Brien pitched after all, and found himself facing Matt McLain — whose grand slam in the sixth, his twelfth homer, had turned a four-to-nothing deficit into the lead St. Louis spent eight innings chasing — with the bases loaded and the game standing on a swing. McLain drove the ball deep to the right-field wall, and Jordan Walker gathered it in for the final out. 'I was very happy with that catch,' O'Brien allowed afterward. 'I was begging him to catch it.'

The ledger will note ten runs in the ninth inning alone, and a symmetry the almanac may never see again: Walker, whose three-run homer in the third — four driven in on the day, four-and-ninety on the season — built the early lead, stood under the ball that ended it; McLain scored the first run of the answering rally and made its last out; and the National's three foremost run-producers — Stewart at six-and-ninety, Walker at four-and-ninety, Burleson at three-and-ninety — were all on the same premises, trading blows. Strzelecki took the decision, Burke the defeat, and O'Brien's three-and-thirtieth save remains the fattest count in the National. The Cardinals, winners of seven in ten, climb to six-and-sixty wins and sit two and a half games from the league's final chair; the Reds — whose Myers, the reader may recall, was the two-homer hero of these very columns on Tuesday — are left eighteen games adrift in the Central, playing, as they have said themselves, for seasons yet to come.

News Around the League

THE MARTE AFFAIR REACHES ITS MEDICAL CHAPTER: AN AUDIENCE AT SALT RIVER FIELDS, AN INFLAMED KNEE, AND TEN DAYS ON THE SHELF

The strangest story of the week, chronicled in these columns since Tuesday's edition, has arrived at something like a resolution. Ketel Marte and his agent sat for several hours Thursday afternoon at Salt River Fields with the Arizona general manager Mike Hazen and manager Torey Lovullo to discuss the events of the past week — the second baseman's failure to appear at Fenway Park on Monday, and his consignment to the restricted list that followed. The magnetic examination of his left knee, forecast in Wednesday's infirmary column, found inflammation, and the club has moved him to the ten-day injured list; because a man cannot be backdated off the restricted list, the sentence runs from Thursday in full. An injection has been administered, and the club's hope is that he returns when the ten days are served, or shortly after. Of the meeting itself, Hazen offered the discretion of a diplomat: 'I'm not gonna get into specifics. I feel like the conversation and meeting was productive... He'll talk to his teammates at some point and we'll go from there.' The Diamondbacks, one game from the National's final chair, will conduct their September with the mystery filed but not fully solved.

THE PROSPECT DESK: SEATTLE REPORTED TO SUMMON THE FINEST PITCHING PUPIL IN ALL THE MINORS

The wires report — by sources, the club not yet confirming — that the Mariners are promoting Kade Anderson, a left-hander of two-and-twenty years who is by the Pipeline scribes' reckoning the best pitching prospect in baseball and the fifth-best prospect of any kind. The figures read like a misprint: across eighteen starts at Double-A Arkansas this season, an earned-run figure of 1.06, with a hundred five-and-thirty strikeouts against a mere thirteen walks in three-and-ninety innings and a third. Selected third overall out of Louisiana State in last summer's draft, Anderson did not throw a professional pitch until this year and has spent the season making the assignment look beneath him. He would join a rotation of Gilbert, Woo, Kirby, and Miller on a club that sits three games from the American's final chair and has just been handled roughly in Milwaukee — which is to say, a club in need of exactly this kind of reinforcement, at exactly this hour. The Cubs arrive in Seattle this evening; the watch begins.

THE MILESTONE DESK MEASURES A ROOKIE AGAINST TED WILLIAMS: STEWART'S SIX-AND-NINETY RUNS DRIVEN IN LEAD ALL BASEBALL

The desk has saluted Sal Stewart's thunder before — his seven-and-twentieth homer turned Wednesday's game in Cincinnati, as this paper recorded — but the arithmetic now demands a fuller accounting. With two more driven in on Thursday, the Reds' rookie stands at six-and-ninety runs batted in through his club's first hundred eight-and-twenty games, the largest figure in either league. Barring calamity he is a near-certainty to become but the seventh rookie of this century to reach a hundred; the seven-and-score plateau of a hundred twenty has been scaled by only seven freshmen since the statistic became official in 1920. And the grandest prize of all is genuinely in play: should he finish atop the major-league table, the Elias scribes certify he would be only the third rookie ever to do it, and the first in six-and-seventy years — Ted Williams led all baseball with a hundred four-and-forty in 1939, and Walt Dropo tied for the lead with the same figure in 1950. The pursuers make the chase delicious: Jordan Walker at four-and-ninety and Alec Burleson at three-and-ninety — the very Cardinals who have spent the week trading blows with Stewart's club, as the morning's lead dispatch attests.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: VLADIMIR'S THUNDEROUS REHEARSAL, GIMÉNEZ'S HAMSTRING, AND A FRIGHTENING PITCH TO MECKLER'S HELMET

The brightest entry issues from Single-A Dunedin, where Vladimir Guerrero Jr., recuperating from the concussion he suffered in a collision at third base a week ago, made his first rehabilitation appearance and treated the Florida State League with appropriate disdain: a run-scoring double struck at nearly nine-and-ninety miles per hour off the bat, two walks, and an early exit with nothing left to prove. The Blue Jays hope to restore him Saturday in the Bronx, the first day he is eligible. 'As soon as he's ready, feeling good and cleared and he feels like he's got his timing, we're going to try to get him back in there,' said the manager Schneider. The same club's ward, alas, admitted a new patient hours later: the shortstop Andrés Giménez left Thursday's victory at the Trop in the fourth inning with tightness in his right hamstring, though an initial examination showed good strength, no magnetic study is scheduled, and the club will see how he feels this day. In Houston, the Angels' rout carried a frightening moment — Wade Meckler took a sinker of better than ninety miles per hour off the helmet in the fifth and walked off under his own power after the trainers' inspection, while Schanuel departed an inning later with soreness in his right side. And the road back grows crowded elsewhere: the wires note Cody Bellinger and J.P. Crawford both began rehabilitation assignments in the minors, each club counting the days.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE PLAYERS TAKE THE WEEKEND, AND WILLIAMSPORT WAITS AT ITS END

This day begins Players' Weekend, the game's three-day exhibition of its own personalities, returned for a third consecutive year with all thirty clubs participating. The program assigns each day a theme — this day the players' pursuits beyond the diamond, Saturday the causes they champion, Sunday an appreciation of those who carried them to the majors — with custom gear on the field and an auction for the faithful who covet it. The desk notes with approval that the programming includes a sit-down between the former All-Star Yonder Alonso and the Reds' young colossus Sal Stewart — celebrated at length in the columns above — on growing up in Miami with Alonso and Manny Machado as mentors, and a tour of Ozzie Albies' fish collection, which the Herald declines to summarize for fear of spoiling it. The weekend closes where this paper has twice said it would: at Williamsport on Sunday, where the Brewers and Braves — who begin their acquaintance this very afternoon in Milwaukee, as the bill of fare relates — repair to the Little League Classic to perform before the smallest and sternest jury in baseball.

The Rest of the Card

TWO THOUSAND NOTCHES AND A TIPPED CAP: RANGERS 2, NATIONALS 0, AND TEXAS RECLAIMS ITS SHARE OF THE CHAIR

The consolation this paper promised Texas yesterday was redeemed with interest. Jacob deGrom opened the evening at Arlington with swinging strikeouts of Lile and Ortiz — the second of them the two-thousandth of his career — and paused, in the middle of the first inning, to tip his cap to a crowd that understood. He then went about the rest of it: ten strikeouts in all across six scoreless innings, one hit and one walk permitted, both to young Brady House, while Seager's thirteenth homer and Lopez's sacrifice fly supplied the whole of the scoring and Latz closed his five-and-twentieth save. The register is worth the ink: deGrom is the five-and-ninetieth man to reach two thousand strikeouts and the second-fastest ever by games and by innings, trailing only Randy Johnson on the one count and Chris Sale on the other, and only the third to strike his two-thousandth in Texas flannels, after Ferguson Jenkins and Cole Hamels. 'Personal accomplishments are cool, but the goal is to win,' said the author, and his club did both: blanked six-to-nothing by Washington on Wednesday, the Arlington men returned the whitewash within four-and-twenty hours and climb back into a share of the American's final chair. 'Today was kind of vintage deGrom,' offered the manager Schumaker, a man who once batted against the original.

TWO-AND-TWENTY FIRST-PITCH STRIKES IN THREE-AND-TWENTY TRIES: BRONX BOMBERS 6, ORIOLES 1, AND COLE PASSES CLEMENS

The broom came out at Camden Yards, and it was wielded by a man of five-and-thirty throwing strike one as no Yankee has in this century. Gerrit Cole opened two-and-twenty of his three-and-twenty batters with a first-pitch strike — the highest such rate of his career and of any Yankee since at least the year 2000, by the researchers' accounting — and struck out eight across six innings of one-run ball, running his count in pinstripes to one thousand and fifteen — past Roger Clemens, at one thousand and fourteen, for twelfth place on the franchise's all-time strikeout table. 'That's the G.O.A.T.,' said Cole of the man displaced. 'That's a big-time name.' The support was ample: three runs in the third upon Caballero's fielder's choice, Rice's single, and Ramos' double, then sixth-inning homers from García Jr. and Jones, with Chisholm's triple cashing a sixth run and Yarbrough pitching three spotless innings for the save. Beavers' homer was the entire Baltimore reply. The Yankees have won four running and hold the American's first wild-card chair at nine-and-a-half games' remove from the scramble below; the Orioles have lost four running and slip two games from the last one.

HOLMES CARRIES NOTHING-AT-ALL INTO THE SEVENTH: ATLANTAS 2, WHITE SOX 0

In a makeup of a June rainout on the South Side, Grant Holmes — whose rotation seat had lately attracted impertinent questions — answered them by flirting with history: no hits through six innings and into the seventh, until Vargas walked and Benintendi lined a clean single, the only safety Chicago would manage all evening. 'Absolutely, I looked at it every inning,' the pitcher confessed of the scoreboard, a candor the Herald prizes. No Atlanta man has thrown a no-hitter since Kent Mercker in April of 1994, and the manager Weiss let him chase it before the walk and the knock made the question moot; Fuentes then struck out three straight to strand the threat, and Iglesias closed his six-and-twentieth save. Riley drove in both runs — a double in the third, a single in the seventh — and Dubón collected three hits. The victory arrests an Atlanta slide of five defeats in six, administered chiefly by Minnesota's sweep, and opens a stretch of three consecutive first-place opponents: two at Milwaukee beginning this afternoon, the Williamsport finale on Sunday, and the champion Dodgers waiting behind them. 'We got a good team, and we're in first place,' said Weiss. 'It's a good group.'

TWO HUNDRED STRIKEOUTS FOR THE MAN NOBODY SHOULD TOUCH: GUARDIANS 5, JINTS 2

The bill of fare posted Gavin Williams and his eleven victories against the Giants, and the big right-hander delivered a twelfth with a flourish: eleven strikeouts across five and two-thirds innings, carrying his season's count to two hundred and one — the first Cleveland pitcher to reach two hundred since Shane Bieber in 2019, and his ninth game of double-digit strikeouts this year, a total exceeded in all baseball only by Misiorowski. 'It's crazy that anybody touches him in the first place,' testified his left fielder Kwan, who spends such evenings largely as a spectator. Adames' two-run homer was the whole San Francisco account against him; Cleveland had built three in the first upon Ramírez's single, Lowe's sacrifice fly, and Bailey's knock, with Kwan and Rocchio adding singles later and Smith closing his two-and-thirtieth save. The victory seals Cleveland's first series in nearly a month — five consecutive sets had been dropped since late July — and the pillowy August schedule this paper once advertised may finally be yielding its comforts: the Guardians sit one game from the American's final chair.

A SEVENTH STRAIGHT SERIES FOR THE SHORTHANDED JAYS: TORONTO 5, RAYS 1, BEHIND BIEBER'S SEVEN INNINGS

The assignment this paper posted for Shane Bieber was executed in full: seven innings of one-run, four-hit ball at the Trop, opposite the same Seymour whose nine victories the bill of fare had advertised, and the Maple Leaf nine had their seventh consecutive series victory — their first taken inside that dome since September of 2023. The blows were distributed among the deserving: Okamoto's six-and-twentieth homer — every one now a fresh extension of the rookie record this paper saluted Tuesday — plus homers from Lukes and Daz Cameron, his first of the season, and Springer's two-run single. 'The Tampa Bay Rays, they always give us problems,' said Lukes. 'But it felt good to finally punch them back.' The performance is the more remarkable for the casualty list: with Guerrero still convalescing and Giménez departing in the fourth with a tight hamstring — both matters detailed in the infirmary column — Toronto executed a full infield line change mid-game, Clement to shortstop, McAdoo to second, Okamoto across to third, and the reserve catcher Valenzuela manning first. Toronto sits half a game from the American's final chair; the Rays, at six-and-seventy wins, remain the league's class and dropped a series anyway.

SIX IN THE FIRST, AND THE RUBBER MATCH IS SETTLED BEFORE SEATTLE SITS DOWN: CREAM CITY NINE 7, MARINERS 4

Two nights after scoring two-and-twenty and one night after scoring five in defeat, Milwaukee decided the deciding game in its opening quarter-hour: six runs in the first against Kirby, built of doubles from Sánchez, Mitchell, and Hamilton and Ortiz's single, before a single Seattle out had much company. Mitchell finished the evening with two doubles, a homer, and three driven in; the Seattle reply — Donovan's two-run double, a passed ball, Canzone's single — reached four before Patrick, Ashby, and Megill barred the remainder, the save Megill's three-and-twentieth. The Brewers thus take the series two games to one and stand at nine-and-seventy wins against nine-and-forty defeats, the finest ledger in baseball by two full games over Los Angeles — and receive the East-leading Braves this very afternoon in the weekend's marquee engagement, of which the desk note sings below. Seattle departs three games from the American's final chair, with its consolation riding in from Double-A: the Anderson summons, reported in the news columns, may put the minors' best arm in a Mariner uniform in time for the Cubs.

WITT STRIKES THE FIRST BLOW AND THE ROYAL BLUES MAKE IT FIVE RUNNING: ROYALS 6, WHITE ELEPHANTS 2

The liveliest August in the American's lower reaches rolls on. Bobby Witt Jr. opened the home first with a homer, his sixteenth, and finished with three runs scored; Perez and Massey collected three hits apiece, Loftin legged out a triple, and Collins drove in two as Kansas City banked twelve hits and its fifth consecutive victory. The remarkable Dobnak — whose 1.73 figure this paper advertised on Wednesday's bill of fare — wobbled through four scoreless innings without a decision, walking four but yielding nothing, and his earned-run mark now reads 1.58; the relief corps of Thomas, Kimbrel, Schreiber, and Pearson did the rest after Duran's brief adventure. The wandering Athletics, whose entire offense was Serven's and Walton's run-scoring strokes, have now dropped four running, and the Missouri engagement continues this evening with the basement's dignity — such as it is — still under negotiation.

EIGHTEEN RUNS, SEVEN OF THEM DRIVEN HOME BY NETO, AND THE WEST'S LEADERS ARE DRAGGED BACK TO THE WATERLINE: SERAPHS 18, ASTROS 3

An offense that had scored three runs or fewer in twenty of its last thirty games chose Thursday night in Houston to spend a month's allowance. Zach Neto supplied a career evening — five hits and seven runs driven in, on singles in the first and fourth, a three-run homer in the fifth, and a two-run double in the seventh — tying the club record for a shortstop's runs batted in that Freddie Patek set in 1980, while the bottom two-thirds of the order went fifteen-for-one-and-thirty. Guzman's two-run homer in the ninth came off the position player Wade Jr., pressed into mound service to stanch the arithmetic, and Rodriguez claimed the victory with seven innings unblemished by an earned run. 'It was so much fun, especially being on the other side of it,' said Neto, whose club took its first road series in nearly three months. For Houston the consequences are the story: at four-and-sixty wins against four-and-sixty defeats the Astros stand precisely at the break-even line this paper has twice marked for them, their lead in the West a single game over resurgent Texas — though the great Alvarez, doubling in his abbreviated evening, still sits atop all three tables of the batter's Triple Crown, his pursuit unbothered by the wreckage around it.

For the fifth morning running the American's final wild-card chair has been rearranged, and this morning it is shared: the idle Twins and the shutout-dealing Rangers sit together at three-and-sixty wins against five-and-sixty defeats — the chair's fifth arrangement in five editions of this paper, after Baltimore's Monday, Tuesday's three cotenants, Texas alone Wednesday, and Minnesota alone yesterday — with Toronto half a game astern despite beating the league's best club, Cleveland one game back, Detroit a game and a half, Baltimore two, and Seattle three, still not one claimant at the break-even line. In the National the seating holds: the Cubs keep the first chair by six games, Philadelphia — winners of six running — the second by two, San Diego the third, with Arizona one game back, St. Louis two and a half after the morning's larceny in Cincinnati, and Miami four. This day's card runs to the full fifteen engagements, all of them dressed in Players' Weekend colors. The bill of fare: at Milwaukee at 4:10, the engagement of the weekend — the East-leading Braves upon the game's best ledger, with Sale and his 2.16 opposite Misiorowski and his 1.75, the two sovereigns of the National's earned-run table, the latter all but measured for his hardware, as this paper reported Tuesday; at Philadelphia at 6:40, the ninth-inning miracle workers of St. Louis call upon Luzardo; in the Bronx at 7:05, Schlittler — proprietor of the American's finest earned-run figure — receives Toronto, with Guerrero hoping to rejoin the visitors Saturday; at Fenway at 7:10, Webb opposes Gray and his fifteen victories; at Seattle at 10:10, the Cubs arrive as the Anderson watch begins; and at Los Angeles at 10:10, the Bucs are examined by Yamamoto. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: 'TWO NUKES IN THE BOTTOM OF THE NINTH': FLORES TIES IT, LOWE ENDS IT OFF THE FOUL POLE, AND THE CORSAIRS SINK THE TIGERS, 4 TO 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 43 · Thursday, the Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

'TWO NUKES IN THE BOTTOM OF THE NINTH': FLORES TIES IT, LOWE ENDS IT OFF THE FOUL POLE, AND THE CORSAIRS SINK THE TIGERS, 4 TO 3

A catcher who did not start the game homers twice from the bench — the second of them to level the affair in the ninth against the great Jansen — whereupon Brandon Lowe's drive drifts toward foul territory, strikes the pole, and settles the evening at a stroke: the first time since 2014 that Pittsburgh has struck the tying and winning blows by homer in the same late inning, on a night the rested Skenes could not command and won anyway

Kenley Jansen has saved more games than every pitcher who ever lived save two, and Wednesday evening at Pittsburgh the whole weight of that eminence could not buy him three outs. The Detroits had done the patient work: the rookie Jackson Jobe outpitched the celebrated Paul Skenes — who was rested expressly for this assignment, as this paper reported Sunday, and repaid the courtesy by wandering the strike zone for four and a third innings, walking four — and a three-to-one lead, assembled from McGonigle's sacrifice fly and double and Gleyber Torres' run-scoring single, was carried carefully to the late innings. Then Rafael Flores Jr., a catcher who had begun the evening on the bench and warmed himself in the batting tunnel against the mere possibility of employment, pinch-hit in the seventh and deposited a hanging cutter from Waguespack over the left-field wall. And in the ninth, with one out and Jansen dealing his famous cutter, Flores confessed afterward to a simple plan — 'ambush' it — and executed the ambush four hundred and thirty-one feet, bat aloft, the game level at three.

The finishing stroke belonged to Brandon Lowe, and to the architecture. The veteran second baseman lifted a fly ball deep down the right-field line, watched the spin carry it toward disgrace — 'all he could do,' the wire observed, 'was pray and watch' — and heard it clang off the foul pole instead. 'I think the wind pushed it back over a little bit for me,' Lowe allowed, in the tone of a man declining to examine a gift. His seven-and-twentieth homer of the year closed the account at four to three, and the record-keepers were waiting at the door: not since the second of May, 2014, when Pedro Álvarez and Starling Marte did the honors, had Pittsburgh struck the game-tying and game-winning homers in the same ninth-or-later inning, and Flores stands as the first Pirate since at least 1900 with two homers in a game he did not start. 'That was a Cinderella story,' said the young man, sensibly. 'Tie game, homer walk-off. That's what you dream of as a little kid.'

Skenes, who had struck out five and left without a decision, claimed a curious clairvoyance: 'I wasn't surprised. I wasn't expecting it to be two nukes in the bottom of the ninth. But I had a feeling that we were going to win that game.' The ledger distributes the consequences evenhandedly. The relief corps of Doval, Weaver, and Montgomery held the deficit at one until the thunder arrived, Montgomery collecting the victory a night after collecting the save; Jansen is charged with his fifth blown save and a fall to three-and-five; and the Corsairs, at three-and-sixty wins, have their second consecutive series in hand while pressing their noses against the glass of the National's wild-card window. Detroit's arithmetic is grimmer still: a second straight defeat leaves the club a game and a half from the American's final chair, which has, as the desk note relates, changed tenants yet again.

News Around the League

THE FRONT-OFFICE DESK: COHEN KEEPS HIS ARCHITECT BUT AUDITS THE BLUEPRINTS — 'TOO MUCH RISK'

The proprietor of the Metropolitans has rendered his verdict on a curious season, and it is a lawyer's verdict: every decision defensible, the sum indictable. Steve Cohen reiterated Wednesday his commitment to David Stearns, the club's president of baseball operations, through next year's campaign — while allowing that the winter's grand renovation carried 'too much risk.' The particulars of that renovation are well known to this desk: a new coaching staff installed beneath the manager Mendoza, Brandon Nimmo traded to Texas for the second baseman Marcus Semien, and Pete Alonso permitted to walk to free agency and into Baltimore colors — whence, as the card below relates, he nearly haunted the Bronx men this very night. 'When you add new players, a coaching staff and adding players with an injured history and you add risk upon risk,' Cohen reasoned, 'it doesn't mean it has to turn out bad... I see individual decisions that make perfect sense. But when you add it all up, did he take too much risk?' The audit arrives, it must be said, just as the books have begun to balance: the Amazins have won eleven of fifteen since the deadline, the rookies Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing supplying the spark, and Cohen permitted himself the small optimism of a man watching young talent arrive ahead of schedule. 'Winning is better than losing,' the owner observed, a proposition this paper has been unable to refute.

THE CLOSER'S OFFICE CHANGES ITS NAMEPLATE IN LOS ANGELES: DÍAZ'S NECK PASSES ITS EXAMINATION, BUT SCOTT KEEPS THE NINTH

The succession this paper reported yesterday is now formalized. Tanner Scott, restored to the closing post upon Edwin Díaz's consignment to the fifteen-day list, is the Dodgers' man for the stretch run by his manager's plain declaration: 'It's easy to say that he's our best reliever and most consistent reliever,' said Dave Roberts. 'I certainly see him as our closer.' The left-hander answered the proclamation Wednesday night with a perfect tenth inning at Denver — eight pitches, seven of them strikes, a day after throwing seven-and-twenty — for his eighteenth save, and his August ledger reads one run allowed in eight appearances. As for Díaz, the news is the best available to a man on the shelf: the magnetic examination of his troubled neck found nothing structural — 'It went well, and there were no findings,' Roberts reported. 'It was a best-case scenario' — though no timetable attends his return, and September is spoken of in the conditional. The wires note besides that the rotation grows crowded with returning eminences, Glasnow's restoration described as near at hand, while Ohtani, as this paper chronicled Tuesday, continues his own long march back to the mound. The champions, in short, are assembling their October inventory.

THE HERALD SALUTES A MAN WHO WOULD NOT STAY DOWN: TOLMAN REACHES THE MAJORS AT LAST, FIVE SURGERIES AND ONE TERRIBLE NIGHT LATER

The freshest name on the Washington roster carries the season's best story. Erik Tolman, a left-handed reliever of seven-and-twenty years, was summoned from Triple-A Rochester this week by way of the traditional ruse — his coaches inquired whether he might fancy winter ball, then whether he might fancy pitching in Texas, which is where the big club happened to be — and the man's path to that little joke beggars belief. Twice his elbow was rebuilt by the Tommy John procedure, once at Arizona State and once more before he had fairly returned. Then, on a night he can date without hesitation — the second of August, 2023 — he hopped the foul line on his way to the mound at Single-A Fredericksburg, caught his spike, and came down into catastrophe: every ligament of the knee torn, the hamstring pulled from the bone, a nerve ruptured, the feeling gone from his foot, and an emergency room where, for five endless minutes, the physicians discussed the possibility of taking the lower leg. 'I've been through a lot,' he offered Wednesday, in the understatement of the young season. 'I was speechless... I haven't stopped smiling today or yesterday.' The Herald, which traffics daily in walk-offs and whitewashes, notes that no score on this morning's card required more of a man than that summons did.

THE PROSPECT DESK READS THE NEW TOP HUNDRED: A BOSTON SHORTSTOP ASCENDS TO THIRD, AND BALTIMORE'S PRIZE FROM THE RUTSCHMAN COMMERCE GATHERS SPEED

The Pipeline scribes have refreshed their register of the game's hundred finest prospects, and the desk extracts three names for the morning reader. First, Franklin Arias, the twenty-year-old Boston shortstop, now third-ranked in all the minors: the young man has struck three-and-twenty home runs this season — more than his first three professional campaigns combined — and is spoken of as potentially the youngest Red Sock to debut since Devers in 2017. Second, Anthony Eyanson, now Baltimore's second-ranked jewel: the desk reminds its readers that he arrived in the very commerce that sent Adley Rutschman to Boston — whose first Fenway thunder this paper recorded only yesterday — and the right-hander has since added two full ticks to a fastball now touching a hundred, with a promising splitter besides. Third, Theo Gillen of Tampa Bay, twelfth on the register, a young batsman whom injury has harried since his schoolboy days and who, at last healthy, is showing why the scouts never wavered. The almanac reader will note the pleasing symmetry: the game's best club and its most patient sellers both grow richer while the season runs.

THE ALMANAC DESK: A FATHER CALLS HIS SHOT IN WISCONSIN, AND WILLIAMSPORT WAITS ON SUNDAY

Two entries, one of them possibly the finest piece of spectating of the year. At High-A Wisconsin on Wednesday, Sawyer Strosnider — Milwaukee's second-round selection of this summer, out of Texas Christian — struck the first home run of his professional life, a changeup dispatched to right-center at a hundred and three miles per hour off the bat. It was caught on the fly, beyond the wall, by his own father. Scott Strosnider, a restless man who tours the stadium during his son's games, had stationed himself on a private party deck and, challenged by its occupants, offered the following credentials: 'Well, my son's about to hit a home run that I'm going to catch.' The prophecy was fulfilled within the minute. 'Right place at the right time,' shrugged the son, who added a run-scoring double for good measure. Second entry, the long calendar: the Little League Classic arrives Sunday, the three-and-twentieth, when the Brewers and Braves repair to Williamsport to play before the smallest and sternest jury in baseball — the same two clubs, the schedule-makers note, who first meet at Milwaukee beginning Friday. The Herald commends the fixture annually and does so again.

The Rest of the Card

THE PALE HOSE ANSWER TWO WALK-OFFS WITH A WHITEWASH: WHITE SOX 3, CUBS 0, AND URQUIDY SPINS A RELIC OF 1991

Twice walked off at Wrigley, the visitors closed the crosstown engagement by permitting nothing whatever. Sean Newcomb opened with two clean innings, whereupon José Urquidy — a man who was not in the organization when these clubs first met in May — struck out eight of the first nine outs he recorded and finished with six scoreless innings on eight-and-sixty pitches, the first White Sox relief turn of such length, so many strikeouts, and no runs since Melido Perez in 1991. 'The secondary pitches, I was spinning the ball well,' said the author. 'I think it was a little confusing for the hitters.' Benintendi singled home the first run in the sixth and Braden Montgomery doubled home two in the eighth before 40,086 souls; Taylor fanned two in the ninth for his seventh save. The North Siders were blanked, and the reader will note what died with the shutout: Crow-Armstrong's pursuit of a third consecutive game opened with a homer, a bid this paper posted on yesterday's bill of fare. The Central's leaders depart with the finale and a cushion of four games; the rivalry, as ever, kept no standings and took no prisoners.

THE NORTH STARS COMPLETE THE SWEEP AND TAKE THE CHAIR: TWINS 6, TOMAHAWK NINE 4

Three days ago Minnesota was licking Philadelphia-administered wounds; this morning, by the geometry only August can draw, the Twins hold the American's final wild-card chair outright. The finale followed the set's pattern of patient larceny: Kody Clemens doubled home two with the bases loaded in the fifth — struck, be it noted, off the left-handed relief summoned expressly to retire him — and, after Atlanta had leveled the affair at four upon Lane Thomas' single, Albies' sacrifice fly, and a balk, Clemens singled home the go-ahead run in the seventh against another left-hander dispatched on the same errand, Brooks Lee adding a sixth for margin. The rookie Kaelen Culpepper, in the majors barely a fortnight, collected his first three-hit game — 'This kid can hit,' said the manager Shelton. 'We knew that when we drafted him' — and Yoendrys Gómez recorded his twentieth save, a third in as many days. Atlanta has dropped three running, its East cushion shaved to four and a half; the sweep's full arithmetic is rendered in the desk note.

THE DESERT NINE REFUSE TO DROWN AT FENWAY: DIAMONDBACKS 7, FENWAY MEN 6, IN TEN INNINGS

A club that had lost its second baseman to mystery and two games to Boston's bats finally planted its flag. Down five-to-two in the sixth after Nootbaar's two-run homer had crowned the visitors' rally, Boston answered through Mickey Gasper — a three-run blow, his third homer in as many nights, a progression this paper has tracked from its first — and the affair went level to the tenth. There Nolan Arenado, jammed, blooped a single to left that scored Moreno, Fernandez walked home a second with the sacks full, and the spare run proved the decisive one when Contreras' groundout drew Boston within a single tally and no closer. 'I couldn't be more proud of these guys,' said the manager Lovullo, whose week has been chronicled in these columns. 'Winning makes all the bad go away.' The victory snaps a three-game slide and pulls Arizona within one game of the National's final chair; as for the absent Marte, this day brings the magnetic examination of his knee and a sit-down with the general manager Hazen — the next chapter, the clubhouse insists, in a saga it has resolved to stop reading.

NOLA JOINS HAMELS IN THE CLUB LEDGER AND THE QUAKERS MAKE IT SIX RUNNING: PHILLIES 4, GULF STREAM NINE 1

The sweep of Miami was completed by the man the season had nearly written off. Aaron Nola worked seven innings of one-run ball, striking out eight — seven of the victims dispatched by the knuckle curve that has lately recovered its old cruelty — for his hundred-and-fourteenth career victory, drawing him level with Cole Hamels for sixth place upon the franchise's all-time table. 'Lately, I've been feeling pretty good, body and arm,' said the author, whose figure across his last five starts sits at 2.51. Arraez supplied the heavy blow, a two-run homer in the third; Turner doubled home a fourth upon an overturned tag play; Sanoja's sixth-inning homer stood as the whole Miami reply; and Duran closed for his eight-and-twentieth save. The defensive jewel belonged to Brandon Marsh, who scaled the left-field side wall like a boy on the Ashburn Alley climbing apparatus to steal a foul pop — aided, he cheerfully confessed, by a spectator who yanked his hat back at the final instant: 'I gotta thank the guy standing over there... I think he had first dibs on it before me.' Philadelphia has won six running, its longest surge of the year, and stands twelve games above the waterline for the first time; the wires add that Nestor Cortes has been fetched from outside the organization to thicken the rotation. The Fish depart four games from the final chair, swept and sinking.

THE OWNER'S FAVORITE ROOKIE SUPPLIES THE PROOF: FLUSHING NINE 4, PADS 2

Hours after the proprietor's musings on risk and youth, recorded in the news columns above, the youth in question filed his brief. Carson Benge struck a two-run homer in the fourth — his fifteenth — and the Flushing nine held the visitors at arm's length thereafter: Tatis' run-scoring double in the fifth drew San Diego within one, whereupon the eighth restored the margin on Bichette's fielder's choice, abetted by a throwing error, and Jared Young's run-scoring single. Sheets singled home a ninth-inning consolation before Senga closed the door. The decision went to the reliever Lavender, his ledger opening at one-and-nought, with King falling to eight-and-nine, and New York claims the series two games to one. The consequences travel west: the Friars keep the National's final chair, but their cushion over Arizona — whose extra-inning deliverance at Fenway is chronicled above — is this morning a single game, and the schedule offers no idle days in which to hide.

A LONG STRIKE, A STOLEN HOME, AND THE HIGHLANDERS TAKE THREE RUNNING: YANKEES 5, O'S 3

The evening at Camden Yards turned upon a ball that did not count. With the affair level in the seventh, Pete Alonso launched a towering drive down the line and set off hopping in the manner of Fisk, certain of the lead; the magistrates called it foul, the replay glass found the pictures inconclusive, and Alonso, howling at the heavens, was thereupon struck out by the untroubled Headrick. 'That's a really defining call in the game,' said the slugger, whose club's own after-hours survey — conducted, remarkably, by the New York replay men plotting the ball's path along the third-base line — concluded the call was correct. New York pressed the reprieve at once: Lombard Jr. legged out a bases-loaded infield single in the eighth and Chisholm Jr. raced home on a bounced splitter — 'We call that the rope-a-dope,' grinned the manager Boone — to break the tie for good. The particulars otherwise: Baltimore's Holliday stole home in the first, straight-up thievery of the oldest kind; Ben Rice answered with his four-and-thirtieth homer; Alonso's nine-and-twentieth had answered in the third, and Beavers' blow leveled matters in the sixth. Bednar closed for his nine-and-twentieth save, the Highlanders' third straight victory, while the O's slip a game and a half from the final chair.

THE TUGBOAT DOCKS, AND THE ORANGE AND BLACK STEAL A WHITEWASH: GIANTS 1, LAKE ERIE MEN 0

The maiden voyage this paper billed yesterday came off precisely to the chart. Matt 'Tugboat' Wilkinson, before some thirty friends and relations in captain's hats, opened the game with two scoreless innings against the very organization that drafted him and traded him away in the Bailey commerce — six of seven batters retired, the celebrated Invisiball cresting at a stately one-and-ninety miles per hour. 'It was definitely a long-awaited moment,' said the debutant. 'I'm happy it could happen here, of all places.' The heavier hauling fell to Adrian Houser, who followed with five-plus scoreless innings and a fastball touching eight-and-ninety — a 0.72 figure now across his last six appearances — for the victory, and Smith barred the ninth. The run, singular and sufficient, was Bericoto's fourth-inning single cashing Devers. The defeat was cruel bookkeeping for Cleveland's Messick, who owns the third-best earned-run figure in the American and fell regardless to nine-and-eight; his club, lately preparing to feast on a pillowy August schedule, was instead handed its own menu.

ELLY'S LIGHTNING, STEWART'S THUNDER, AND THE QUEEN CITY NINE COME FROM BEHIND: REDS 5, REDBIRDS 4

Cincinnati's evening displayed all three of its crown jewels in a single setting. Chase Burns, laboring without his sharpest edge, ground through five innings of two-run ball with eight strikeouts — 'Just grinding, mentally,' the All-Star allowed. Elly De La Cruz, ranging into short right-center as the relay man, threw a runner out at the plate at 99.2 miles per hour — the fourth-fastest infield assist the measuring machines have recorded, the man himself owning the first three — to keep a scoreless game scoreless. And the rookie Sal Stewart, with St. Louis ahead two-to-nothing in the sixth, struck a three-run homer, his seven-and-twentieth, to turn the ledger over entirely. The Redbirds made it interesting to the last: Jordan Walker's two-run blast in the ninth, his five-and-twentieth, drew within one before Pagán shut the door behind Moll's victory. The clubs part with the season's series concluded and their wild-card errands diverging — St. Louis three chairs' lengths from the last seat, Cincinnati playing, by its own admission, for seasons yet to come.

SEVEN EARLY, SIX SURRENDERED, ONE HELD: GULF COAST CLUB 7, CANADIANS 6

The league's best club continues to win in the manner of a man carrying soup down a staircase. Tampa Bay built a seven-to-one lead by the fourth — Yandy Díaz's two-run homer to open, then a five-run frame composed in the club's signature miniature: a fly ball the Toronto left fielder Sánchez misjudged into a two-run gift, back-to-back bunts by Walls and Simpson that each cashed a runner, and Caminero's groundout — whereupon Toronto spent five innings clawing it back through Kirk's homer and singles beyond counting, McAdoo's double drawing the visitors within one in the sixth. There the arithmetic froze: Rasmussen had done enough for his thirteenth victory, Baker barred the late innings, and the Rays had their eighteenth one-run decision of the season. 'If we win, it doesn't matter,' shrugged Rasmussen, a philosophy his club at six-and-seventy wins can afford. The defeat fell to Scherzer, whose ancient shoulders bore yesterday's billing opposite Rasmussen and now a ledger of one-and-six; the Jays slip a full game from the final chair.

SEVEN IN THE EIGHTH AND THE KANSAS CITY NINE MAKE IT FOUR RUNNING: ROYALS 9, MACKMEN 7

For five innings the wandering Athletics played the better game, McNeil twice driving home runs and a five-to-one lead in hand; then the Kansas City eighth arrived like weather. Seven runs crossed in the frame: Pasquantino — who had homered in the sixth and now singled home another — Isbel's knock, Collins' sacrifice fly to level the affair at five, and then the decisive stroke, John Rave's sharp three-run double that emptied the bases at a blow, Garcia singling home the seventh behind it. Muncy's two-run homer in the visitors' ninth dressed the final margin at nine-to-seven. The victory — Kansas City's fourth running, the liveliest August in the lower reaches of the American — went to the ancient Kimbrel, and the clubs conclude their set this afternoon with the basement's dignity, such as it is, at stake.

THE PAGE IS TURNED WITH SEVEN RUNS IN TWO INNINGS: PUGET SOUND MEN 7, SUDS MEN 5

The response to the worst defeat in a franchise's history was delivered before Milwaukee had fairly taken its seats. Seattle sent all nine men to the plate in the first — Canzone's two-run double and Ward's two-run single the heavy freight — and stacked three more in the second upon Rodríguez's sacrifice fly and Naylor's two-run knock, seven runs that chased the Brewers' starter May before the second inning was done. 'We had our teeth kicked in yesterday,' said Donovan, who reached base four times at the head of the order. 'So I guess it's just how you respond.' The response required defending: Joey Ortiz answered with a homer, a sacrifice fly, and a run-scoring single — three driven in — and Milwaukee crept within two by the eighth before Muñoz closed the door. Gilbert took his tenth victory, and the clubs settle the rubber match this very afternoon at the scene of Tuesday's crime. The Brewers, at eight-and-seventy wins, keep the game's best ledger by a game and a half over Los Angeles; Seattle departs the evening having proven, at minimum, that the page turns.

SEVENTEEN INNINGS OF NOTHING AND COUNTING: CAPITAL NINE 6, LONE STAR NINE 0, AS CAVALLI FANS ELEVEN

The finest pitching of the night was done in Arlington, where Cade Cavalli struck out his first seven outs entire — eight strikeouts by the end of the third, ten by the end of the fourth on a mere sixty pitches — and finished with eleven across six scoreless innings, his shutout streak now standing at seventeen. The register notes that since the franchise came to Washington, only Scherzer and Roark had fanned ten inside four innings; Cavalli, with his eighth consecutive quality start and a 2.12 figure across ten outings, is pitching himself into that company by the week. 'It's just a testament to the process,' said the author. 'Not riding the highs, not riding the lows.' The margin was supplied late: Tena's homer and small carpentry made it three, and Andrés Chaparro broke the evening open with a three-run blow in the seventh. For Texas the defeat was doubly dear — blanked at home, the Rangers surrender the wild-card chair they had held alone but a single morning, and slip two games behind Houston in the West besides. The almanac offers them one consolation: deGrom takes the ball this evening.

A DEBUT, A BULLPEN OF IRON, AND THE STREAK IS ENDED: HOUSTON NINE 3, HALOS 2

The West's leaders arrested their three-game slide by the narrowest sufficient means. The rookie Ethan Pecko, ninth on the club's prospect register, made his major-league debut and battled through three and two-thirds untidy innings — 'It was a little sloppy, but I felt like I battled,' the young man reported, with a candor the Herald salutes — whereupon the relief corps of Sousa, Blubaugh, Okert, Abreu, and Hader delivered five and a third scoreless innings, the continuation of a bullpen ledger that reads 2.21 since late July, the best figure in the game. Vázquez homered, Altuve doubled home the equalizer, and Cam Smith's sacrifice fly supplied the difference; Anaheim's runs had arrived on Guzman's double, awarded amid fan interference. Hader closed, Sousa took the decision, and Houston, at four-and-sixty wins, holds the West by two full games over silenced Texas — with the great Alvarez, whose pursuit of a crown of three this desk charted yesterday, scoring the tying run in workmanlike anonymity.

THE SOUVENIR-CATCHER TAKES THE VICTORY: ANGELENOS 6, MILE HIGH NINE 4, IN TEN, AND THE SWEEP IS NINE

The tenth inning at Coors belonged to the professionals: Freeman's sacrifice fly cashed Pages, Betts singled home Teoscar Hernández behind him — three hits and two driven in for the great shortstop — and Los Angeles had its ninth sweep of the season. The record-keepers append a curiosity: the Dodgers stand four-and-nothing in extra innings, the only club in baseball yet to lose one. Roki Sasaki, crowded into anonymity by his own rotation's eminence, supplied five innings of two-run ball — a 2.31 figure now since the All-Star pause — while Betts' sixteenth homer and Enrique Hernández's two-run blast had built the early lead; Moniak's twentieth leveled matters in the seventh before the extra frame. And the victory itself went to Kyle Hurt — the very reliever who, two nights ago in these columns, caught Ohtani's four-hundred-fifty-two-foot homer in his bullpen glove; the man has now collected a keepsake and a decision from the same week's residency. Scott's perfect eight-pitch tenth, saluted in the news columns, sealed it. The Angelenos, at seven-and-seventy wins with three straight victories and forty of them earned on the road — no club has more — depart Denver a game and a half behind Milwaukee for the game's best ledger; Colorado's consolation is that the caravan has finally left town.

The arithmetic desk reports that the American's final wild-card chair has now changed occupants on four consecutive mornings: Baltimore held it Monday, three tenants shared it Tuesday, Texas sat alone Wednesday, and this morning it belongs to Minnesota — the sweep of Atlanta complete, a half-game clear of the blanked Rangers, with Toronto a game astern, Cleveland, Baltimore, and Detroit a game and a half, and Seattle two and a half: the chair's fourth tenant in four editions of this paper, and still not one claimant at the break-even line. In the National the seating holds but tightens: the Cubs keep the first chair by six, Philadelphia the second by two, San Diego the third, with Arizona now a single game back of the Friars, St. Louis three, and Miami four. This day's card runs to nine engagements, the schedule-makers granting the rest of the company a travel day before Friday's full slate. The bill of fare: at Cincinnati at 12:40, McGreevy opposite Singer in the set's conclusion; at Cleveland at 1:10, Williams and his eleven victories receive the Giants; at the Trop at 1:10, Bieber takes the ball for Toronto opposite Seymour and his nine-and-three; at Kansas City at 2:10, the remarkable Dobnak — a 1.73 figure — opposes the Athletics; at Chicago at 2:10, the East-leading Braves arrive on the South Side for a cross-league examination of the Central's leaders, Holmes against Kay; at Milwaukee at 2:10, Seattle and the Brewers settle their rubber match, Kirby opposite Gasser; and in the evening, Cole at Baltimore at 6:35, deGrom against the streaking Cavalli's Washingtons at 8:05, and the Angels at Houston at 8:10. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
